title: We say we value diverse research, but can we assess it?
summary: Research outputs come in all shapes and sizes, and the REF process acknowledges. But, as Ola Thomson and Gemma Derrick's research demonstrates, we're still not clear how non-traditional outputs can be fairly and consistently assessed
full_text:
When you think about a research output, do you think of a journal article?

If the answer is no, then it’s great that you recognise research diversity. If the answer is yes, then this is understandable given the deep embeddedness of papers and articles in knowledge production and evaluation.

Despite the dominance of the written research output form (articles, books, conference proceedings), there is a diverse range of outputs currently being produced by researchers that don’t neatly fit current academic evaluation approaches. Such formats, or non-traditionally submitted outputs (NTOs) can include datasets, websites, software, artefacts, digital or visual media, design, research reports and all other outputs. Despite taking time, expertise and considerable time to produce, they are not appreciated as valuable records of research excellence.

While the 2029 REF is strongly encouraging the submission of diverse research output, and indeed “outputs” has been renamed “contributions to knowledge and understanding” (CKU) which echoes this commitment, our most recent research shows that the REF approach to assessment remains unprepared for NTOs.

Why aren’t NTOs put forward in REF submissions?

Part of the problem with bringing NTOs into mainstream research submission practice is a lack of experience in evaluating them. Previous REF exercises showed the dominance of journal articles and books as preferred measures of outputs; these represented over 97 per cent of the output types submitted in the REFs 2014 and 2021, and a similar proportion in earlier research assessment exercises. The REF Main Panel D reigns supreme in the submission of diverse outputs, but the other panels (A, B, and C) are lagging behind, partly because of disciplinary differences.

The other, not unrelated part of the problem, is that this under-representation of NTOs in formal evaluation processes also means there is a lack of widely shared tools that evaluators can use to assess them. This lack of experience in evaluating NTOs means that the criteria used for evaluating all outputs are well suited to the majority, but less so for the remaining three per cent of diverse output types.

The under-representation of NTOs in previous exercises is not the fault of the REF. Indeed, NTOs have long been considered as eligible for inclusion in REF (and RAE) submissions, but HEIs have been reluctant to include them, even when they are appropriate to the field. It has not gone unnoticed that computer science – currently assessed as part of UoA 11 – has never evaluated a dataset or piece of software during REF.

Part of the reason for this is in how the competitive instinct of HEIs overrides the REF’s objective to assess a diversity of research outputs. When compared to journal articles or books, a university is unable to confidently replicate the REF evaluation process internally for NTOs. This lack of knowledge of how to benchmark NTOs internally prior to submission results in a perceived risk from NTO submissions that is simply too great.

What the hidden REF is doing

The E-TIE project funded by Research England is currently working to bridge the chasm between a lack of socialised experience in evaluating NTOs, and a lack of evidence to do so effectively. Through the Hidden REF competitions, festivals, and NTO workshops currently being conducted around the country, the team has conducted a series of ‘think-aloud’ studies that track how evaluators approach the assessment of NTOs using REF criteria.

In these mock REF evaluations, participants are presented with an NTO and are asked to actively record how they reasoned the assessment of an NTO, rather than report their choices retrospectively. It is an effective way of asking participants to consciously value NTOs in the form they are presented to the REF; as well as understand how the REF 2029 CKU criteria of significance, originality, and rigour can be applied.

If you can’t see the research, you can’t assess it

We found that the difficulty isn’t just with how evaluators apply REF criteria to NTOs, but also with how they are submitted to the REF. Submissions can (but don’t have to) be accompanied by a 300-word description where the research is not obvious within the output itself, or they can be bundled into portfolios of outputs and submitted as the “other” category. However, NTO submission choices, approaches, and tactics vary widely depending on the submitting HEI and their different interpretations of the REF guidelines.

Unfortunately, while journal articles embed a description of the research process within the methods section (or other familiar structures), NTOs often need additional translation or information concerning how the research conducted contributed to the output presented. Between NTO types, a description of the research itself is inconsistent and often underspecified.

This means that evaluators struggle to separate an assessment of the excellence of the research process from an assessment of its contribution to knowledge, and, in turn, makes it harder to apply any traditional academic criteria (whether REF-based or not) consistently between NTOs and traditional outputs. Instead, evaluators will repeatedly ask for more context or explanation beyond what is provided in the submission itself. Where the link between research process and output was unclear, we found that evaluator scores dropped even where the quality of the research may have been high.

Three criteria, many interpretations

The REF criteria (originality, significance and rigour) matter, and they are easily applied to journal articles or books. Their relevance to NTOs, however, was more uncertain: evaluators treated significance, originality, and rigour as flexible tools rather than fixed standards. Instead, evaluation outcomes were shaped by the interaction between the reviewer and the submission, not just the framework, with the REF criteria acting as scaffolding.

Criteria were applied inconsistently, and only to the extent the output allowed for it based on the limited information provided. In many cases, REF criteria were either partially used or bypassed entirely. For example, originality was difficult to interpret for some output types, and rigour became dominant because it was easier for participants to anchor to other aspects such as funding, partners, or scale of the research. Significance, on the other hand, was often reduced by participants to a question of “how international is it?”

Remarkably, evaluators drew on a broader and more varied cornucopia of evaluative principles as criteria. Judgements around notions of ethics, appropriateness for the audience, reach, scope, or team science surfaced repeatedly, suggesting that the value of NTOs was appreciated by criteria other than those provided by the REF to evaluators.

“Is this even research?”

Evaluators used multiple, but inconsistent, cues beyond the provided REF criteria to judge NTO quality. These cues, such as institutional prestige, links to journal articles, social or policy impact, and download or usage metrics, were not logically linked to the REF criteria. In some cases, these heuristics or practical cognitive shortcuts, which can help make decisions efficiently, teased at the boundary of what is considered responsible and irresponsible research evaluation.

In situations where the evaluation cues are not widely socialised, such as when evaluating NTOs, the use of these heuristics is understandable and has been seen previously in the evaluation of (then) new criteria such as impact (for instance, in Derrick, 2018).

When compared to the heuristics socialised to match a valuation of journal articles via set criteria any uneven or else inappropriate proxies used to evaluate NTOs jeopardise the integrity of the REF evaluation process. The use of inappropriate proxies is more acute for NTOs because evaluators aren’t always familiar with the output type (even if they are discipline experts) and is particularly notable in those disciplines where NTOs are more prominent. In disciplines where the boundaries between research and artistic practice become blurred (as one participant stated; “…is this even research?”), evaluation becomes more uncertain. Here, the evaluation process still produces a score, but what drives that score goes beyond the criteria provided by the REF, and is instead improvised.

This prompts us to ask whether the REF criteria for CKU are fit for the purpose of NTO evaluation, or are we asking a rich and varied research culture to squeeze through a very narrow gate designed only for journal articles and books?

From inclusion to recognition

The challenge is not simply whether the REF encourages us to include NTOs (it very much does), but whether we believe NTOs can be evaluated in ways that are consistent, fair, and trusted, so that they are considered less of a risk to included in the first place.

At present, the REF criteria for CKU are tried and tested for traditional outputs but are not suited for NTOs. So, on one hand the REF wants to encourage more NTOs to be submitted, but NTOs need to be submitted to a system that is ill-equipped to evaluate them fairly, with very real consequences. The combination of uneven submission practices, flexible interpretation of criteria, and reliance on informal proxies risks cementing uncertainty in the process and with it, institutional caution. The result is a system that encourages diversity in principle but continues to reward familiarity in practice.

There is hope, however, and with the REF still in the criteria-setting stage ahead of publication in “autumn”, adjustments to the evaluation criteria for NTOs are needed. These adjustments would include criteria that would evaluate NTOs on their own terms rather than on terms that are set for a traditional output.

Without NTO-specific evaluation guidelines, we are unlikely to see HEIs put more NTOs forward as part of their submission. This would be a missed opportunity, not only to construct NTO-relevant evaluation criteria, but also would limit our understanding how a diverse range of output types contribute to the UK research sector.

title: Ghent professors challenged expertise of Jason Arday’s plagiarism accuser
summary:
Allegations Nathan Cofnas was unqualified for Ghent role and would cause ‘negative impact’ made to senior leaders months ago

Nathan Cofnas, the academic who accused Jason Arday of plagiarism, has been accused of having “very limited expertise” for his academic role by professors also working at Ghent University, who say he has a “far-right agenda”.

Cofnas secured a postdoctoral research role “on the future of liberalism” at Belgium’s Ghent University in March. Weeks later, Ghent’s department of philosophy and moral sciences handed a 19-page statement to university officials, setting out why it believed it was “improbable” that Cofnas was the best candidate.

Continue reading...
full_text:
Nathan Cofnas, the academic who accused Jason Arday of plagiarism, has been accused of having “very limited expertise” for his academic role by professors also working at Ghent University, who say he has a “far-right agenda”.

Cofnas secured a postdoctoral research role “on the future of liberalism” at Belgium’s Ghent University in March. Weeks later, Ghent’s department of philosophy and moral sciences handed a 19-page statement to university officials, setting out why it believed it was “improbable” that Cofnas was the best candidate.

Jason Arday, the University of Cambridge sociology professor, was found dead on 14 August after weeks of intense media scrutiny of his professional and personal achievements following Cofnas’s allegations against him of plagiarism, which have not been formally proven.

Allegations that Cofnas was not qualified for his research role and would cause a “negative impact” by promoting racial pseudoscience were made to university leaders months before Arday died, the Guardian understands.

Cofnas’s online activity promotes pseudoscientific ideas of racial difference between Jews and non-Jews and Black and white people. In 2023 he wrote on X: “There are obviously personality differences between Jews and non-Jews … On average, Jews are better than gentiles at capitalising on their [general intelligence].”

In a statement sent to the university’s rector on 28 May, Ghent’s philosophy department said: “We find it very improbable that Nathan Cofnas was the best out of 14 candidates … We observe only very limited expertise regarding the subjects that are central to the project: political philosophy, liberalism and demography.

“The formulated requirement in the job posting of a ‘strong research interest in liberalism’ is not borne out by Cofnas’ publication record or the rest of his CV.”

Academics alleged there had been a lack of transparency around the appointment of Cofnas and that “a large majority” suspected he had been “an ideological choice … decided in advance”.

In the statement to Ghent’s rector and the faculty dean, which the philosophy department’s council approved as its “official position” on 27 May, academics said: “Cofnas himself has never conducted research on intelligence, nor is such research envisaged within the project for which he was hired.”

They added: “The views he disseminates [in blogposts] are not based on his own scientific research … [and] simply not based on sound research.”

The statement followed an email sent in March to university leaders and governors, signed by 48 department staff, 73 students and 367 academics from Ghent and other universities expressing “astonishment and indignation” at Cofnas’s appointment.

A spokesperson from Ghent University said they did not comment on “the specific details of the disciplinary case or the underlying arguments”.

Last week, the university said it had suspended Cofnas pending a “preliminary investigation”. The university did not say whether the suspension was over allegations related to Cofnas’s appointment. In a joint statement confirming the suspension, Ghent’s rector, Petra De Sutter, and vice-rector, Herwig Reynaert, said: “We attach great importance to academic freedom and to open academic debate, even when views are controversial. However, that freedom is not unlimited.

“It goes hand in hand with responsibility and may be restricted in order to protect the rights of others. The university takes the recent public statements made by a postdoctoral researcher at Ghent University regarding this matter very seriously. Ghent University has decided to take appropriate action within its powers and the applicable framework.”

In an April 2023 Substack post titled “How to take back academia”, Cofnas outlined ways to “remove” academics he described as “wokesters” by “showing that they don’t satisfy minimal criteria”.

In response to allegations of plagiarism, Arday, whose treatment has been described as a “racist feeding frenzy”, admitted “mistakes”, but said he had faced unacceptable cruelty.

A source said: “Jason was the most gentle, generous, encouraging person. He wanted to bring communities into the academic space. He was working constantly for others.”

More than £224,000 has been raised for a fund set up by the cultural historian Sir Patrick Vernon to help support Arday’s grieving family. In a statement they said they were “deeply moved”, adding: “The response to this appeal reflects the number of people whose lives were touched by our beloved Jason and the affection, respect and admiration in which he was held.”

Responding to the allegations over his appointment, Cofnas said: “My academic qualifications are a matter of public record.”

He added: “The silliest accusation is that I am ‘uninterested in the academic exchange of ideas’. The people who said this are trying to get me fired or even thrown in jail for expressing my ideas.”

title: The Fight for Fair Funding at One Historically Black Land-Grant University
summary:
The Fight for Fair Funding at One Historically Black Land-Grant University
Olivia.sanchez Thu, 08/27/2026 - 03:00 AM

A new book from the former president of Tennessee State University reveals her battle to regain $544 million in documented underfunding.

Byline(s)
Olivia Sanchez
full_text:
Tennessee State University is one of the most underfunded historically Black land-grant universities in the country. In a 2023 letter to Tennessee Governor Bill Lee, former Education Secretary Miguel Cardona and former Agriculture Secretary Tom Vilsack said the state owed the institution more than $2 billion, accrued over the past three decades.

According to another tally in 2021 from the Tennessee Office of Legislative Budget Analysis, the state owes the university anywhere between $150 million and $544 million in unpaid land-grant funds over the last 50 years.

The state report set off an advocacy campaign to recoup the unpaid money. At the center of the fight was TSU’s then president, Glenda Baskin Glover. In 2023, the state invested $250 million in the college, but Glover and other advocates said it wasn’t enough to stabilize the struggling institution or make up for the decades of underfunding.

In her new book, How Dare You: A University President’s Fight for Half a Billion Dollars Owed—and the State’s Actions to Avoid Payment, Glover gives an account of how she learned about the structural deficit and her fight to recover the funding. Glover led TSU from 2013 to 2024, a period of financial instability and controversy, including a year when TSU enrolled more students than it could house and had to put hundreds of students in hotels. The debacle led the state comptroller to call for a change in leadership in March 2023. Glover retired the following year after receiving a contract buyout, according to local news reports.

In her book, Glover offers her side of the story. She covers the historical background of structural underfunding at TSU, how the Black Lives Matter movement influenced the funding discussion, her view of state audits and what the path forward for the college might look like. She said she hopes the book will put the university’s budgetary situation in context and dispel the idea that the university’s financial stress was a result of mismanagement by her administration.

“I love my university. It shaped my thinking, grounded my values, and helped make me the leader I became. This is not about a fight with TSU—it’s about my fight for TSU,” Glover writes. “What this book reveals is not simply an injustice in funding, but the machinery that protected that injustice. It details the decisions, omissions, and calculated maneuvers used to keep TSU from receiving the funds it was owed—allowing a century of inequity to continue without accountability.”

Glover spoke with Inside Higher Ed about her book and her tenure at TSU. This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Q: You say in the book that you wanted to put the truth about what happened at TSU on the public record. What is the biggest misconception about your presidency that you want this book to correct?

A: I think the biggest misconception that I want to correct is the belief that Tennessee State University had a severe financial crisis and that there was overspending and administrative failure. There was not.

The crisis was caused by more than two decades of state underfunding, structural underfunding. This was created long before I arrived and it was documented repeatedly during my tenure. TSU did not lose any money. The state withheld it. TSU did not create a deficit. The deficit was imposed on TSU. TSU was forced to operate without the funds it was legally owed. So TSU’s financial instability was never an internal failure—it was a predictable result of external neglect that came from the state withholding funds.

My presidency was defined by stability in the face of deprivation, not mismanagement in the field of abundance. So, to me that’s the biggest misconception that needs to be corrected.

That the narrative surrounding all the charges or comments that were made by the comptroller and others, that narrative is focused on the symptoms rather than the cause. The cause was underfunding.

Q: When describing your first 100 days on the job, you said you were warned to tread carefully and avoid getting on the wrong side of state leaders. How did you interpret that advice, and did it shape how you approached the presidency?

A: I was warned not to get on the bad side of certain legislators. They gave me some names, but honestly I don’t remember them. I was happy to hear any information I received.

But I didn’t get on the bad side of legislators. I did not. What I did was insist consistently, professionally and factually, that Tennessee State University receive funding it was legally owed. Some people interpret that insistence as a conflict. It was not a conflict; it was accountability. I was warned not to press too hard, not to ask for too much, not to challenge the status quo. But the truth is simple: I did not oppose legislators, I opposed underfunding.

The Morrill Act said both state land-grant universities had to be equitably funded. That was my challenge. So I didn’t create any tension. The tension was already created between what was owed to TSU and what TSU received. My responsibility as president was to advocate for the institution.

Q: You argue that TSU’s financial difficulties have to be understood in the context of decades of underfunding. How do you distinguish between problems caused by that structural underfunding and problems for which your administration should be held accountable?

A: There are things that TSU could have done better and so we take responsibility for that. For example, the housing problem that they used as a smoke screen. It was a good problem. We had so many students who wanted to attend Tennessee State University. That should have been celebrated, and the state should have worked with TSU to ensure that we had adequate housing.

We had a place on campus that used to be a residence hall that we were using for classroom purposes; we considered using that temporarily. They said no to that. We went to Texas to look at manufactured housing, and we came back and presented that as a temporary option. They said no to that. The third option was the hotels, so we pursued the hotels. Other universities—other HBCUs—were doing it, so we didn’t think we were out of order.

What the Legislature didn’t understand, and refused to do, was to separate housing from education. We were able to serve the students to make sure they got their classes. We had more adjunct professors. We did everything within the rules of making sure students were educated and we could accommodate them.

Q: You’ve now had about two years away from the presidency. Is there anything you would do differently if you could go back to 2022 or 2023?

A: I would communicate earlier and more forcefully about the decades of underfunding that shaped TSU’s financial reality. I would have framed the issue not as a budget challenge but as a structural injustice, one that required statewide partnership and not institutional blame. And I would have insisted that the conversation begin with the context that the financial difficulties were the predictable results of long-term underfunding, not any short-term decisions.

Now, had that context been established earlier, the narrative surrounding TSU would have been clear, would have been fair, would be more accurate. So, the only thing I would change is not the advocacy, not the leadership, not the decisions, but the timing and framing of the truth.

Q: What do you think the state should do now—not just about the money, but about the relationship between Tennessee and TSU? Is it possible to repair it?

A: Well, the relationship with TSU and the state was good until we started pressing for the money. TSU does not need punishment. It needs parity. It does not need scrutiny, it needs support.

And the state should acknowledge the decades of underfunding, correct their structural deficit that they keep maintaining with TSU and commit to a predictable funding model that allows TSU to thrive as the state’s only public HBCU. You know, this is not to blame, it’s just the truth. Healing begins with recognition.

I don’t think a relationship is beyond repair. But they have to treat TSU as a partner in statewide economic development. TSU produces the teachers, the nurses, engineers, entrepreneurs, the public servants. Supporting TSU is supporting Tennessee. As of now, the debt is still not paid.

title: Commencement Speakers’ Politics Vary by Institution Type
summary:
Commencement Speakers’ Politics Vary by Institution Type
Johanna Alonso Thu, 08/27/2026 - 03:00 AM

A new study from researchers at Georgia State and New York Universities finds that commencement speakers skew liberal. But the type and location of the institution can make a difference in who is invited to speak.

Byline(s)
Johanna Alonso
full_text:
David Johnson’s interest in the political leanings of commencement speakers was sparked in 2020, when a podcaster he was listening to asserted that conservatives “aren’t welcome” on college campuses.

“I thought, that doesn’t resonate with me. At minimum, it sounds not terribly nuanced,” recalled Johnson, a sociologist and associate professor of higher education in the Department of Educational Policy Studies at Georgia State University.

To understand whether conservatives are, in fact, welcome onto college campus, he decided to analyze the one occasion when nearly every college or university invites a speaker onto campus each year: graduation.

“There are all sorts of different speech events that happen across the system of higher education, like invited speakers and colloquia and universitywide speaker series,” but those events can vary a lot from institution to institution, he said. “Commencement, however, is universal.”

His research builds upon the debate over whether liberal ideology is overrepresented on college campuses, including evidence that faculty members and college administrators skew to the left. But while that research investigates how the people who work in higher education lean politically, Johnson was interested in understanding whom colleges choose to bring to campus to represent the institution at commencement, one of the most important days of the academic year.

In a paper published this month in the American Educational Research Journal, Johnson and his co-author, Liang Zhang, a professor of higher education at New York University, found that commencement speakers tend to lean liberal. But that picture is complicated by factors like the location and size of the institution and whether it’s a private or public university.

Graduation has been a flashpoint for universities in recent years; the Class of 2026 protested or pushed their institutions to disinvite speakers over their stances on Israel, artificial intelligence, the late conservative commentator Charlie Kirk and more. Students have also used commencement as a time to protest their own institutions; in 2024, amid widespread protests over Israel’s bombardment of Gaza, some graduating students interrupted ceremonies to call for their institutions to divest from companies with ties to Israel.

Commencement speakers are often the most prominent and high-stakes guests an institution invites each year. Whom they choose, then, can serve as an indication of what an institution values and how they want to be perceived, the researchers argued.

Using a database of 35 years of speakers at 52 institutions, cross-referenced with public information about those speakers’ political donations, Johnson and Zhang found that public colleges were more likely than private ones to invite speakers who supported conservative candidates, as were colleges that focused more on occupational and professional programs. Meanwhile, institutions that enrolled more students of color and those with larger endowments were more likely to select liberal-leaning speakers. Unsurprisingly, the state’s political leanings also had an impact; institutions in blue states tended to invite more left-wing speakers, and the same was true for conservative speakers in red states.

“What this tells me is that universities are strategic and they’re trying to maintain legitimacy in the eyes of a diverse public and a diverse set of internal stakeholders: students, faculty, boards, the public and governments,” Johnson said. “Universities are trying to navigate this era of polarization and look legitimate in the eyes of everybody.”

The report, which examined speakers through 2024, also found a statistically significant increase in liberal speakers over time, particularly after 2011.

“This shift coincides with a rise in left-initiated disinvitation campaigns,” the authors noted in the report, as well as “growing partisan polarization, and an intensifying national debate over the role of higher education in American political life.”

The researchers also found that disinvitation campaigns, in which students or other stakeholders call on the university to revoke their invitation to a graduation speaker, are effective over the long term, if not immediately. Although only two of 34 campaigns were actually successful in having the speaker disinvited, the researchers found that in the years following such a campaign, colleges throughout the state proved more likely to choose speakers that align with the campaigners’ ideology over several years. In other words, if students tried to have a speech by a conservative speaker canceled, future graduation speakers within that state were more likely to be liberal.

Free speech organizations like the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression have criticized colleges for disinviting commencement speakers, arguing that doing so teaches students the wrong lesson about how to handle being confronted with difficult or controversial ideas. The organization has documented 382 commencement speaker disinvitation campaigns since 1998.

Johnson doesn’t think institutions select speakers based on their actual political donations, of course. But they probably seek out speakers who are as uncontroversial as possible.

“I think that they are trying to select somebody who reflects well on the university, makes them look prestigious or who happens to uphold something amazing to their students,” he said, “but also do that in a way that avoids political controversy.”

title: New Paper Takes Aim at ‘Meritocratic’ Admissions Policies
summary:
New Paper Takes Aim at ‘Meritocratic’ Admissions Policies
kathryn.palmer… Thu, 08/27/2026 - 03:00 AM

Wealthy students with high standardized test scores make up the majority of students at the most selective universities, which also spend far more on student instruction than less selective institutions. So where does that leave everyone else?

Byline(s)
Kathryn Palmer
full_text:
Despite the Trump administration’s claims that some of the nation’s most selective colleges have admitted legions of students with low test scores to advance racial diversity, new research shows that’s largely not happening.

Instead, a working paper published by the National Bureau of Economic Research this week used decades of federal data to lay out the reality: The most accomplished high school graduates—who tend to come from higher-income families—make up the vast majority of students enrolled at the nation’s best resourced, selective public and private institutions. Meanwhile, their peers with lower standardized test scores, who are more likely to come from lower-income families, more often end up at higher education institutions that spend far less on each student’s education—if they go to college at all.

For example, in 2019, spending on per-student instruction increased 29 percent for every 100 average SAT points of enrolled students, according to the report. At the same time, roughly two-thirds of students at Ivy League and other top-50 private universities—and more than half of students at state flagships—came from families in the top income quintile. Income distributions of students at less selective public and two-year colleges were broader and more reflective of national income distributions.

Given those disparities, “it’s high time we interrogated what we are doing with this admissions system,” Jesse Rothstein, director of the Center for Studies in Higher Education at the University of California, Berkeley, and co-author of the paper, told Inside Higher Ed.

“The Supreme Court’s Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard decision or the attacks on DEI presume that the only legitimate way to do things is to admit the students with the highest SAT scores,” he said. “Arguably, what you should be doing is admitting the students who have the most ability to benefit, and it’s not at all clear that that’s best captured by prior achievement.”

But even as selective institutions have become more reliant on using test scores as an admissions metric over the past 50 years, the resource gaps between the wealthiest universities and the rest have widened.

In 1969, per-student instructional expenditures at the most selective institutions (enrolling the highest-testing students) were about double the expenditures of the least selective colleges.

By 1993, more selective colleges were spending 150 percent more per student than the least selective colleges. By 2019, they were spending 200 percent more. According to the paper, the widening gap came during “a period of substantial state disinvestment from public higher education in terms of states’ block funding allocations.” Universities that admitted higher-testing students “were relatively more successful at privatizing and raising greater replacement revenue from their students,” and also used private gifts and government research contracts to subsidize instructional activities.

Though resource stratification across universities has leveled off over the past decade, in large part because of increased public funding for less selective colleges, disparity within institutions is on the rise as the more lucrative majors are increasingly adopting supplemental achievement-based admissions policies.

‘Meritocratic Consensus’

The paper describes the widespread acceptance of this resource stratification as “meritocratic consensus,” which Rothstein argues is overdue for reconsideration.

“It’s taken for granted that the objective of college admissions is picking out the smartest students, and that somehow it will all be better for everybody if they go to the most selective schools, and the students who aren’t as well prepared go to less selective schools,” he said. “There’s just not much evidence for that assumption.”

But there is evidence that higher per-student spending is associated with higher graduation rates and higher-paying jobs, he said. The additional resources that would be most beneficial to cash-strapped, open-access institutions vary by institution but could include “smaller class sizes, better facilities and better support for students to help them navigate the school and get them through their program,” Rothstein said, noting that less selective colleges serve students that often need those resources the most.

“If you take a straight-A student and send them off to college, they probably are going to be just fine when they get into a college class,” he said. “But if you take a student who struggled in high school and send them to college, they may need a little bit more scaffolding and support to get through college. Tutoring, mentoring and support programs are very effective, but they cost money.”

Spending money to close the disparities between the most selective and least selective institutions is key to raising the college-attainment rate nationwide, he added.

“If we really think that the route to a middle-class job is for everybody to get a college degree, then we need to make it feasible for students to get college degrees who were not the top of their class in high school,” Rothstein said. “If in fact it’s the case that more resources spent on lower-achieving students would be productive, then we’re leaving a lot of value on the table by not doing that.”

title: Behind the Scenes of the College Presidency
summary:
Behind the Scenes of the College Presidency
sara.custer@in… Thu, 08/27/2026 - 03:00 AM

For three years, The Sandbox has revealed a side of higher education leadership most of us will never see.

Byline(s)
Sara Custer
full_text:
Inside Higher Ed’s reporting on the college presidency is investigative and holds leaders to account. But three years ago we created a space where anyone who wants to know what’s happening behind the scenes of the college presidency can learn directly from the people on the job. The Sandbox is our weekly serving of real, anonymous essays from higher ed leaders, and it goes where our journalism can’t.

Co-created, curated and edited by Rachel Toor, a writer who has been in higher ed for more than 40 years and worked in every corner of the sector from academic publishing to admissions to her current job as a professor of creative writing at Eastern Washington University, this Saturday-morning newsletter is where leaders get vulnerable about the challenges of the job, big and small. Anonymity allows them the safety to write freely and, because they’re not identified in any way, strips away higher ed’s entrenched institutional hierarchies: There are more similarities in the experiences of a community college president and an Ivy League leader than you might think.

Having covered higher ed for 15 years, I speak to leaders all the time and hear about the problems they encounter. I’ve learned from reading The Sandbox, though, that there are conversations with presidents I don’t have. Nor should I, as a journalist. But The Sandbox gives me a glimpse into the human side of the job.

Reading how many leaders endure death threats, sexism from donors and board members, and attacks on their children, it’s no wonder the average tenure for a college president is now little more than five years. For women and presidents of color, it’s even shorter. With state and federal funding cuts, remnants of a global pandemic, transformative federal policy changes, existential threats from artificial intelligence, and low public confidence, the pressures on presidents have only increased. Higher ed needs leaders who will stick around to carry it through this time of crisis. The essays in The Sandbox make clear the personal challenges that the job also requires them to endure.

Don’t confuse personal stories as a plea for sympathy, though. The presidents who write for The Sandbox are not asking us to feel sorry for them. They know what they’re getting themselves into. Their essays offer insight to a side of the job most of us will never see. Here are a few things I’ve learned about the college presidency from over 150 college leaders from every part of the sector.

Presidents are on all the time, and though they may appear polished and collected, for many it’s a slog. They work hard to build their networking skills and resiliency. One president wrote, “What I did not expect was the emotional toll of having others look to me for validation, vindication, and acceptance. As president, you are the symbol of the institution—a living mascot. One donor said, after chatting with me at a football game, that he felt like he’d ‘just met royalty.’” Leaders feel they are expected to always have the answer “and be willing to have pies thrown at you at any moment—whether at a board meeting, the Rotary Club, the Faculty Senate, or while out walking your dog.”

They’re surrounded by people and are lonely. Though they all have teams, it’s often a one-person gig. One wrote that loneliness is “a feature, not a bug, of the job.” They often don’t have confidants who can be their thought partners. The people they work most closely with are either their bosses—the board—or people they supervise, the cabinet. A theme that comes up regularly in The Sandbox is how devastating those relationships, when they’re bad, can be to a person’s ability to lead.

While presidents have thousands of peers, they struggle to be honest when they’re around each other. Read Inside Higher Ed for a week and you’ll learn how many institutions face low enrollment and money problems. Yet, as one author wrote, presidents in the company of other presidents aren’t forthcoming with the problems on their campuses. “Being a president is exhausting. Being around other presidents? Maybe even more exhausting. Not all of us, but definitely too many of us, can’t turn off the posturing. And being around that posturing, especially when behind closed doors, can really deplete me.”

Spouses and partners are expected to play the role of first gentleman or lady. Presidents write about the guilt of dragging their families into the job. While leaders accept their grueling schedules and being always on call, many boards also want their president’s spouse, who often has their own career and own identity outside the institution, to be a living mascot, too.

Their children are thrust into the spotlight, and their behavior scrutinized. One president wrote that after their relationship with the board deteriorated, some members went after their children. “They were attacked by these grown-ups and could not talk to their friends about what was happening,” the president wrote. “They had to cope without peer support. They were collateral damage in the board’s war on me, which made me feel awful and responsible. Worse, they thought if they did something—anything—wrong, it might be the final straw that cost me my job.”

Presidents and their families are often the targets of harassment and threats of violence, more often than most of us ever hear about. One president wrote that they have received two death threats and two threats of physical harm. “‘They will get you in a small room and won’t let you out’ and ‘This place will look like Columbine and Virginia Tech,’” the message threatened. They had been stalked for years, had a permanent restraining order against someone and one family member was “confronted by an employee brandishing a large knife offering to ‘slit your throat.’”

Female presidents write about double standards, obsessions with their appearance, comments about their clothing, weight and hair color. And they’re expected to carry out emotional work in ways their male predecessors never had to. One female president wrote that the tension between her gender and the responsibilities of the job “is part of my existence.”

“There are plenty of presidential training programs, but how many of them teach women how to negotiate in a predominantly male profession where the single most important part of your job is to raise funds while patiently faking smiles as you are mansplained to again and again,” she wrote. “My accomplishments feel nonexistent when I’m trying to avoid that creeping hand.”

A Black female president said she has grown into a leader who says things that many people—women, especially women of color and folks who are otherwise marginalized—cannot say. “Now I am willing to go into spaces and say that I see a therapist regularly, that constant code-switching takes a mental toll, that I get exhausted even when I appear indefatigable, and that sometimes it takes great effort to appear incessantly joyful and cheerful,” she wrote. “I do get tired of people feeling that I should take care of them when no one had such expectations of my male predecessors.”

But despite the mental and emotional toll of the presidency, leaders love their jobs. As one person told Rachel, “It’s hard, but it doesn’t suck.”

Many Sandbox authors write that the students invigorate them. Move-in days and commencement ceremonies make it all worth it. They marvel at living in houses they would never be able to afford on their own, though they often discover things like black mold, ancient plumbing and bats.

Some of them remain scholars at heart and love to geek out about the arcane research on their campuses. One wrote that the best thing about the job is “going to fantastic lectures in cool fields you haven’t studied by scholars who are interesting and smart and make you wish you could go back to school.” Another president said, “I learn about difference-making research happening on our own campus that I had zero clue about. The place is a treasure chest, and sometimes I don’t even know where the keys are until someone hands them to me.”

In just three years, Rachel has built a growing community of hundreds of current and former university presidents who are willing to tell hard stories that are usually only shared over drinks with close friends. Some say they find the writing therapeutic. As Rachel says of the personal, first-person perspective she pushes authors to take, “It’s the vivid and specific details that make us feel the lessons being imparted.” Those personal experiences that few of us ever see or hear about are an essential bit of knowledge if we want to truly understand the college presidency and the current challenges in higher ed.

title: AI Tends to Mark Students’ Essays Higher Than Humans, Study Shows
summary:
AI Tends to Mark Students’ Essays Higher Than Humans, Study Shows
Susan H. Greenberg Thu, 08/27/2026 - 03:00 AM

LLMs cannot be relied on to give accurate indication of student performance, researchers find, as universities explore ways to relieve pressure on graders.

Byline(s)
Juliette Rowsell for Times Higher Education
full_text:
Artificial intelligence tools typically award higher marks on average than humans and cannot be relied on to give an accurate indication of a student’s performance, according to a new paper.

With AI increasingly being explored by universities as part of the marking process to relieve pressure on time-strapped academics, the research, published in the journal Assessment & Evaluation in Higher Education, found that generative AI tools such as ChatGPT “do not reliably reproduce human judgement in the marking of extended written work.”

The researchers uploaded 50 undergraduate bioscience essays to two versions of ChatGPT and asked it to grade the essays against seven assessment criteria under four different prompting conditions. They found “significant discrepancies” between AI-marked essays and those graded by humans.

In all but one case, the AI models typically returned higher average marks than humans. In one case the difference between an AI grade and a human one was 40 points for an essay where the top score was 100.

Lower-scoring essays tended to receive inflated marks, whereas higher-scoring essays received lower marks compared with human assessment. AI was more aligned with human markers on midgrade essays.

The study says that the large language models tested “varied considerably” in marks awarded, and “were inadequate predictors of the human mark awarded to essays.”

“Despite being relatively consistent at producing similar marks when using the same prompt on the same essay, when used to mark a range of essays of differing standards, there was poor alignment between the LLM-provided marks and the marks assigned by the original human marker. Although the ‘overall’ mark[s] for the essays were relatively well aligned on average with human marks, differences for individual criteria were considerable, reflecting the aggregating effect of a composite score,” it says.

The research was primarily motivated to evaluate whether generative AI could be used as a formative benchmarking tool for students, in addition to feedback from academics, rather than whether it could replace human markers.

Report co-author William Kay, senior lecturer in statistics (teaching and scholarship) at Cardiff University, said he had never questioned that responsibility for marking should remain a human one, but the study underlined that fact: “At present, GenAI is unable to reliably assign a mark to a subjective piece of written work comparable to that of humans—even with extensive training of the LLM,” he said.

“While there is interest across the sector in whether the pattern-recognition capabilities of LLMs could facilitate objective grading of students’ work, making marking more efficient and relieving pressure on staff, the findings of this research indicate that at present this is not advisable. Aside from the ethical issues of submitting student work to GenAI tools without express consent, LLMs cannot, and should not, be relied upon for assigning grades to extended written work by students.

“As LLMs become more sophisticated, it is possible that in the future their ability to mimic human judgment may enhance. But, as we find in this study, aligning marks between humans and GenAI may be hard to achieve,” Kay said.

The paper notes that LLMs might be better equipped to predict “extreme” marks if grading criteria is more detailed and uses “objectively distinct descriptions for each mark bracket,” rather than relying on terms like “good, excellent, outstanding,” which “may be challenging for LLMs to differentiate.”

Although it concludes that “as LLMs become more sophisticated, their ability to mimic human judgement may enhance,” it adds that “high levels of inter-rater variation among human markers” could make this alignment “hard to achieve.”

title: School districts face a back-to-school math problem: The high price of diesel
summary: With the war in Iran driving up fuel prices, diesel is now nearly $5.60 a gallon, affecting school districts at the start of the year.
full_text:
Catch up on what you missed with our Education newsletter, sent weekly.

As the new school year kicks off, school districts are facing a challenging math problem: the high cost of diesel.

The price of a gallon of diesel is up nearly $2 compared with this time last year. That is meaningful for schools, considering that around 90% of the United States' 480,000 school buses run on diesel.

Nationally, the average price was $5.62 for a gallon as of Wednesday, according to AAA. This time last year, it cost $3.70.

School districts nationwide have been wrestling with the issue since spring, when the war with Iran started and fuel prices rose. A May survey produced by organizations that represent school superintendents and bus companies found that more than half the districts surveyed said diesel prices were already pushing them over budget.

In Washington state, Jacob Kuper, the Yakima School District's assistant superintendent of finance and operations, estimated that in the 2026-2027 school year, the higher cost of diesel could cost his district 38% more — or $130,000. "The equivalent of one teacher," he said.

So he looked for ways to reduce the district's diesel use. And he found a few: The district consolidated bus routes. It staggered bell times, reduced the number of total trips and put more kids on the same bus. "So then you save on the actual number of drivers you need," he said.

Kuper said that with those efforts, they're on track to save more money — about $400,000 to $500,000.

But as kids head back to school for the fall, those changes could still pose some problems. "You have fewer drivers with longer routes or longer total hours per day," he said. That means more difficult days for drivers.

Still, Kuper considers the Yakima School District lucky. "We're fortunate we have a small geographical footprint," he said, compared with more rural districts. Yakima's routes aren't that much longer, he said, so kids don't have to spend much more time waiting on a bus.

The May survey found that 40% of school districts were also consolidating their bus routes. About 20% reported they were limiting non-required trips, like field trips. Others said they were considering switching their yellow buses to non-diesel vehicles.

Now, as schools reopen, districts will have to look for other ways to cut expenses, said Elleka Yost, director of advocacy and research at the Association of School Business Officials International, one of the organizations that conducted that survey. "Many districts are tapping reserves or rainy-day funds as a temporary solution," she wrote by email to NPR. But, she added, this may weaken districts' ability to respond to future financial challenges.

In Boise, Idaho, the school district has also looked for ways to reduce the number of stops per route. "Every stop adds mileage and cost," said Lanette Daw, the district's transportation supervisor. The district also added eight electric buses to its fleet this week, funded by a federal Clean School Bus Program award, as the district explores whether this could help save on fuel costs long term.

Still, the district's transportation costs are higher this year: an increase of about $600,000.

In Monterey, Calif., Tom Thorpe, the school district's transportation director, said he is watching prices "carefully, conservatively." And he's not just watching diesel: Monterey has transitioned most of its 50 or so school buses from diesel to gasoline. But state and local taxes make gas prices in Monterey higher than the national average. On Wednesday, the average price of gas in that city was $5.77 per gallon, while the national average was around $4.10, according to AAA. That makes gas in Monterey potentially more expensive than diesel elsewhere.

Thorpe saw this problem coming. By the end of the last school year, "I knew I wouldn't have enough money," Thorpe said. The district tried to make its routes as efficient as possible, but he said, "Buses get full. Ridership time is a concern."

So he talked to his boss. " I actually had to go back twice and say, 'I didn't project enough, boss. Can we get a little bit more?'"

But, he quipped, "my boss is a nice man." He got the money he needed, he said, and "we squeaked through the rest of that quarter."

Going forward, Monterey — as well as other school districts — will continue combing through their budgets, searching for things they can do without and put toward fuel use instead.

In Washington, Kuper will keep wrestling with his district's fuel costs. He said his job is to keep the buses rolling, to keep the district on budget "and keep the reductions outside the classroom, if possible."

title: Meet Lennox French, student whose VR classroom idea won state approval
full_text:
French’s journey started in the Spark Lab at Lexington Senior High School, where students are encouraged to explore emerging technologies and to build ideas that have real-world applications.

A high school student's vision of a virtual classroom is about to go far beyond the walls where it started. Lennox French, a student at Lexington Senior High School in North Carolina, has been chosen to develop and implement a virtual-reality learning unit that could soon be available to students across the state. The project is a first for SparkNC, making French the first student in the program’s history to create a unit for its statewide platform, states the school website report.

From a student project to an idea for the whole state

French’s journey started in the Spark Lab at Lexington Senior High School, where students are encouraged to explore emerging technologies and to build ideas that have real-world applications. French created a first version of a virtual-reality Spark Lab last year. His project investigated how immersive digital environments could offer new avenues for students to learn, collaborate and explore. Now the concept is in a position to reach a much larger audience, rather than being confined to a school-based experiment. French will put together a unit called Creating Digital Spaces in VR, which will take his original idea and create a structured learning event for Spark Scholars across North Carolina.

Project approved by state review

The proposed course had to be reviewed by the North Carolina Department of Public Instruction before the unit could continue. The department has determined Creating Digital Spaces in VR conforms to the state’s computer science standards. Therefore, the unit satisfies SparkNC’s alignment requirements for aggregation to course credit. That approval is a big step in turning French’s student project into an educational tool with statewide importance. For Garland Beamer, a Spark Lab leader at Lexington Senior High School, the decision is also a landmark step for the school and its student innovation program.

The student becomes the designer

What’s interesting about French’s project is he’s not just learning to use virtual reality. He is helping to design the educational experience. In the coming months, French and Beamer will work with NCDPI, SparkNC, industry stakeholders and technology companies to flesh the concept into an engaging and practical unit. That collaboration will include refining the content, technology and learning experience so students outside of Lexington can use the platform effectively. SparkNC Executive Vise President and Co-Founder Joe Ableidinger also acknowledged the work behind the project and expressed support for the development process.

The classroom reimagined

The use of virtual reality as an educational tool has been researched for a long time, allowing students to engage with simulated environments rather than simply viewing information on a screen. French’s project takes that idea a step further by putting a student at the center of the design process. The aim is not just to use VR technology, but to teach students how digital spaces can be built and used for learning. This may allow Spark Scholars to develop technical and creative problem-solving skills as they learn about an emerging area of technology.

From Lexington to North Carolin...

The project also highlights the opportunities for students to play with technologies that are still revolutionizing education and industry. An idea born in a Spark Lab in a high school is now being scaled for students across an entire state. It shows how innovation driven by students can help expand educational opportunities for Lexington Senior High School. For French, the next few months will be spent developing an idea into an operational learning unit. His project started with the idea of a classroom in virtual reality. Now that classroom could be a shared educational experience for students well beyond his own school. Images Courtesy: istock and Lexington Senior High School

End of Article

title: Australia: Carolyn Evans warns of fallout from further international student cuts
summary:
Universities have been pushed into reliance on international student income by years of public funding cuts, Universities Australia chair Carolyn Evans has warned, saying any reduction in numbers must come with a plan for the financial fallout.

The post Australia: Carolyn Evans warns of fallout from further international student cuts appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
Delivering her State of the Sector address at the National Press Club on August 25, Evans suggested the debate over international students had become too simplistic.

“There may be good reasons for reducing the number of international students,” she said, “but we need an honest and informed policy debate about the consequences.”

Evans, who is stepping down as vice-chancellor of Griffith University and will soon take up the role at the University of Melbourne, said universities had been pushed towards international recruitment to fill funding gaps created by government policy.

“Generating revenue from international students was the only realistic solution,” she said.

“A lot of public discourse likes to describe this as universities being greedy, risky, and addicted to international student funding. We are, in truth, forced by government policy to be reliant on it.”

She warned that radically reducing international student numbers could have consequences far beyond university balance sheets.

“So, you can have or promote a policy to cut international student numbers radically but at the same time, what’s the plan for the financial sustainability of our universities?”

“Will the taxpayer resume responsibility for them or will we as a nation happily see thousands more job losses and the closure of small campuses?”

She also questioned the impact on sectors that rely heavily on international students and graduates.

“And what of the consequences to our tourism industry which gets the benefit of friends and family visiting students in Australia?” she said.

“And what are the long-term diplomatic consequences if young people in our region go to university in China rather than Australia?”

Evans argued that governments should be prepared to confront those trade-offs openly rather than treating student-number reductions as an isolated migration-policy measure.

“At the end of all that analysis, a government may still want to deeply cut international student numbers for other worthy reasons,” she said. “But at least people will be eyes wide open that along with the positives they have been promised, there are negative consequences as well.”

Evans used the second half of her address to make a broader argument for greater university autonomy, calling for legislative protections against government overreach.

“The second set of changes I would like to see is the creation of both legislative settings and a public culture which ensures universities have sufficient independence and autonomy,” she said.

She argued that autonomy was not simply a matter of universities protecting their own interests, but a safeguard for democracy.

Having autonomous universities is also an inherent good – a critical protection against creeping authoritarianism and populist pressure

Carolyn Evans, Universities Australia chair

“Having autonomous universities is also an inherent good – a critical protection against creeping authoritarianism and populist pressure,” said Evans.

“A thriving liberal democracy requires a range of strong, independent institutions to stand between the significant power of the State and the relatively powerless individual.”

She warned that increasing regulation, new federal bureaucracies and political pressure were narrowing the space for universities to operate independently.

“The cumulative cost of this approach needs tallying, and there needs to be a reckoning,” she said.

Evans acknowledged that autonomy could mean universities making mistakes, but argued that centralised control could make those mistakes systemic.

“If you give Australia’s forty odd universities freedom, some will make mistakes,” she said.

“But some universities will try something innovative that succeeds beyond all expectations.”

“If, however, you try to control too much from the centre and the government or ATEC gets it wrong then every single university will make the same mistake.”

Evans ultimately called on the federal government to legislate protections for university autonomy.

“I am calling on the government to consider legislative protection for university autonomy,” she said, “to help stem the tide of government overreach.”

She conceded that universities still needed regulation and accountability, particularly over public money, but said the balance had shifted too far towards intervention.

“There is a place for regulation, for accountability, and a reasonable debate to be had at where the limits of university autonomy end,” said Evans.

“But I fear at present, there is no debate at all – just an endless sense that whatever regulation seems expedient can be introduced and that it will not prove a menace.”

title: Teaching With Humanity: What Students Need Most in the AI Era
summary:
We have to talk about what it’s going to mean, in an increasingly AI-saturated landscape, to teach without AI. Because one thing it won’t be is what we’re used to.  As we know, many people have serious concerns about the rapid spread of this new technology through our educational spaces. Some cite the wide array of dangers (environmental, economic, cognitive, democratic, etc.) it poses; others are skeptical of the wealthy and unregulated corporations designing and aggressively disseminating AI; […]

The post Teaching With Humanity: What Students Need Most in the AI Era appeared first on Faculty Focus | Higher Ed Teaching & Learning.
full_text:
We have to talk about what it’s going to mean, in an increasingly AI-saturated landscape, to teach without AI. Because one thing it won’t be is what we’re used to.

As we know, many people have serious concerns about the rapid spread of this new technology through our educational spaces. Some cite the wide array of dangers (environmental, economic, cognitive, democratic, etc.) it poses; others are skeptical of the wealthy and unregulated corporations designing and aggressively disseminating AI; still others simply note that there’s a lot we don’t know about this technology, and that we need to approach it with caution rather than a rush to implement. Altogether, many of us are saying—at the very least—slow down.

This is an uphill battle, perhaps, and one that might take a while. In the meantime, though,

I’m arguing that we need to do something that sounds simple, but isn’t: we need to learn how to teach without AI. And the reason that this isn’t simple is because teaching without AI means—has to mean—something different from what it used to mean back when this tech was unavailable.

Teaching without AI can’t, for example, mean ignoring these developments and pretending like we live in the past. No, we all have a responsibility to know what AI is and what it might be doing to the world—and, in particular, to our students.

After all, these new tools claim to offer a lot of appealing stuff: ready answers, speedy information, a lightened workload, and even therapy, medical advice, spiritual counsel, and companionship. Those offerings may be shaping many students’ experiences and expectations, all of which they’ll bring into the classroom. Against this backdrop, we’ll need to be particularly alert to signs of student distress. And it’ll be important for each of us to find out exactly what our individual students are bringing—surveying them, having full-class and individual office-hours conversations—so that we can respond with the most effective and transformative learning opportunities possible.

We also need to know what AI promises in the educational sphere, because some of those benefits are worth pursuing—by humans, without AI. In particular, advocates claim that AI has the advantage of being able to personalize learning, tailoring the journey to each student’s needs. That’s a great idea, actually, so we need to make changes in our institutions and classrooms to shape learning around our students’ diversity and individuality. How much agency, for example, can we give students to identify their own learning goals in our courses and to design course-relevant projects of personal importance? How responsive can we be to their individual challenges and progress, creating somewhat different arcs for each student?

Teaching without AI also can’t mean just returning to old practices. In fact, we have to confront the likelihood that those practices apparently did not make a sufficiently convincing case for the importance of human struggle, discovery, and growth. If they had, we might not now be dealing with ubiquitous arguments about the supremacy of efficiency, a flood of misinformation and disinformation, and persistent offers to take meaningful labor off our hands.

If a process of struggle, discovery, and growth does matter to us, we need to make space for all of it in our schools. Some of this is out of an individual teacher’s control: every student is dealing with a pile of obligations, social, professional, and academic, only some of which are coming from that one teacher’s course. One broader question for higher education, then, is: what are we asking of our students, and do our demands leave room and time for expansive learning?

But there are things we can tackle in the classroom. In what new ways can we offer our students low-stakes opportunities to experiment, make mistakes, hit dead-ends, try again, try again, and try again? This is a good argument for implementing multiple smaller assignments rather than a small number of big ones, for breaking major projects into discrete parts, and potentially allowing students to redo assignments in order to improve.

How can we better help students experience and explicitly reflect on the pleasure of reaching understanding after a messy, winding path? First of all, foregrounding our own reflective practices—both as we do our work and as we observe students doing theirs—creates a model for them to emulate. If informal reflection prompts aren’t part of your assignments, consider including them. Meetings with individual students, when possible, would allow that reflection to happen in conversation. We can also guide them to focus their reflection on key issues: the connection between discomfort and breakthrough, the value of doing the work oneself—even difficult or mundane work—at each stage of the process, and so on.

Of course, we can add extrinsic motivation, too, by rewarding students for throwing themselves into the work via process and completion grading. We all ought to be asking ourselves: to what extent does my grading system privilege outcomes, and to what extent does it value the process of learning?

Altogether, teaching without AI can’t just mean teachers slapping tools out of students’ hands. There’s plenty of reason to eschew this technology, but our approach can’t be, in other words, just about the exclusion of a technology. Teaching without AI in this moment has to be about thoughtfully promoting teaching and learning that is powerful, personal, meaningful, and lasting. It’s got to mean teaching with, and for, humanity.

David Ebenbach is the author of twelve books of fiction, non-fiction, and poetry, including his new collection The AI Suspects It Might Be a Hungry Ghost. He teaches creative writing and literature at Georgetown University’s Center for Jewish Civilization and creativity through GU’s Learning, Design and Technology Program, and he’s the Assistant Director for Graduate Student and Faculty Programming at Georgetown’s Center for New Designs in Learning and Scholarship.

References

Boehm, Jessica, Russell Contreras, and Isaac Avilucea, “AI arrives at church: How chatbots are shaking up religion.” Axios Phoenix, November 17 2025. https://www.axios.com/local/phoenix/2025/11/17/churches-ai-sermons-prayer-apps

Corrigan, Paul T., “A Taxonomy of Harm for the AI Age.” Inside Higher Ed, June 10 2026. https://www.insidehighered.com/opinion/views/2026/06/10/taxonomy-harm-ai-age-opinion#

Cox, Jay, “The Rise of AI Companionship: Exploring love, loss and ethics in the age of artificial intelligence.” Syracuse University, January 28 2025. https://www.syracuse.edu/stories/ai-at-ischool/

Frances, Allen and Luciana Ramos, “Preliminary Report on Chatbot Iatrogenic Dangers.” Psychiatric Times, August 15 2025. https://www.psychiatrictimes.com/view/preliminary-report-on-chatbot-iatrogenic-dangers
